Width is VARIABLE on the wire; the declared width is a drawn placeholder — read the real extent from the label, never from this figure's widths

svg.metadata:
# FigDown — figures as text. Spec: https://github.com/FigDown/figdown
figdown 0.1 bitfield
# QUIC Long Header — Initial Packet # RFC 9000 §17.2 / §17.2.2 # Each row is 32 bits, MSB-0 numbering (bit 0 at left).
# Six of this header's fields are VARIABLE-length on the wire and v0.1 has no # RANGE width (`BITFIELD-RANGE-WIDTH`): three connection-id/token regions and three varints. # Until this release they carried invented widths (24, 24, 24, 8, 16, 16) with # nothing in the model to say so, and `note="padded to 24 bits for display"` # — a renderer's excuse in a channel that does not draw. The `*` budget is one # per block and it is spent on Payload, so the honest move available in v0.1 # is to DECLARE the fabrication: the real extent goes in the label, and the # class meaning (which IS in the model, §12.7) says the number is a drawn # placeholder rather than a width. class varlen "Width is VARIABLE on the wire; the declared width is a drawn placeholder — read the real extent from the label, never from this figure's widths"
bitfield quic_initial "QUIC Long Header — Initial Packet (RFC 9000)" word=32 numbering=msb0
# ── Byte 0: First Byte (8 bits) ────────────────────────────────────────────── # Abbreviated labels for 1-bit/2-bit cells (each cell is 1/32 of row width): # H=Header Form F=Fixed Bit PT=Long Packet Type Rs=Reserved PN=Pkt Num Len field H:1,F:1,PT:2,Rs:2,PN:2
# NO `break` HERE, AND THIS IS LOAD-BEARING. A QUIC long header is not # word-aligned: Version begins at bit offset 8, immediately after the first # byte, and every field below it starts at an offset that is not a multiple of # 32. A `break` after the first byte would end the drawing row and leave bits # 8..31 blank. The language is right that those blank cells are not bits — but # a reader does not read the source, and 24 blank cells inside a header row # read as padding. That is a FALSE STATEMENT ABOUT THE WIRE, and it is a # different thing from the `varlen` fiction below: `varlen` declares its # placeholder in the model, whereas blank space declares nothing and is simply # believed. Until this release this file had the break, so every offset in the # figure was 24 bits too high — a reader computed DCID Length at byte 8 when # it is at byte 5. Do not re-add it.
# ── Version (32 bits, starting at bit 8) ───────────────────────────────────── # Spans the end of the first 32-bit word: bits 8..39. The renderer draws a # wrapping field as the name on the first row and `(cont.)` on the next, which # is the RFC's own convention for a field that does not fit the remaining row. field "Version" 32 fill=#dbeafe description="0x00000001 = QUIC v1"
# ── Destination Connection ID ───────────────────────────────────────────────── field "DCID Length" 8 field "Destination Connection ID (0-160 bits, 0-20 octets)" 24 class=varlen description="length is carried in the preceding DCID Length field — RFC 9000 §17.2"
# ── Source Connection ID ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── field "SCID Length" 8 field "Source Connection ID (0-160 bits, 0-20 octets)" 24 class=varlen description="length is carried in the preceding SCID Length field — RFC 9000 §17.2"
# ── Token (Initial packets only) ───────────────────────────────────────────── field "Token Length (8/16/32/64 bits, varint)" 8 present="Initial packets only" class=varlen description="RFC 9000 §16: a variable-length integer is 1, 2, 4 or 8 octets" field "Token (variable)" 24 present="Initial packets only" class=varlen description="length is carried in the preceding Token Length field — RFC 9000 §17.2.2"
# ── Length + Packet Number ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── field "Length (8/16/32/64 bits, varint)" 16 class=varlen description="RFC 9000 §16: a variable-length integer is 1, 2, 4 or 8 octets" field "Packet Number (8-32 bits, 1-4 octets)" 16 fill=#d1fae5 class=varlen description="length is 1 + the two-bit Packet Number Length in the first byte — RFC 9000 §17.2"
# ── Payload ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── # No `break` here either, for the same reason. It used to be harmless — with # the break above, the cursor happened to land on a word edge here, so it # added nothing. Once the first break went, this one became the same defect # moved down the figure: it would leave the 24 bits after the Packet Number # blank. The payload begins immediately after the packet number, so `*` fills # the remainder of THIS row and says so. field "Payload" * description="protected"
